en: Title: *Devātiśayastotra* (also known as *Devatāvimarśastuti*) Author: Śaṃkarasvāmin (variants)

Source: Schneider, Johannes. 2014. *Eine buddhistische Kritik der indischen Götter: Śaṃkarasvāmins Devātiśayastotra mit Prajñāvarmans Kommentar, nach dem tibetischen Tanjur herausgegeben und übersetzt*. Wiener Studien zur Tibetologie und Buddhismuskunde Heft 81. Vienna: Arbeitskreis für tibetische und buddhistische Studien, Universität Wien. [Sanskrit updated edition on pp. 163–167]. Tibetan: D 1112.
Input: Péter-Dániel Szántó, Budapest, December 26, 2023.
Oṃ! Homage to the Lord, the Glorious Perfectly Awakened One!
The Blessed One, the Sugata, is not perceived by direct perception, nor are Viṣṇu, Hara, or Hiraṇyagarbha;
yet their excellence of form, conduct, and power—
Having heard it, one examines whether it possesses merit or not. || 1 ||
Viṣṇu has a hand terrible with a raised mace-weapon; Śambhu wears a garland of skulls with human heads attached;
but Buddha is characterized by the excellence of his supremely peaceful conduct.
Whom shall we worship—him who is inwardly tranquil, yet appearing in an untranquil form? || 2 ||
Viṣṇu became the destroyer of the lineage of Duryodhana and others; indeed, Hara was the destroyer of Tripura;
and Guha likewise struck down Krauñca with his firm spear.
But the Buddhas alone are those who desire the welfare of the world. || 3 ||
"This person must be oppressed by me, this one alone must be protected,
and this one must be slain"— this is the policy of the best of gods,
whose intellect is solely intent on the welfare of the happiness of both ultimate liberation and worldly prosperity.
For the Buddha, there are no enemies, nor are there any who can deceive him. || 4 ||
The words of Viṣṇu give rise to defects such as passion;
those of Śambhu produce the behavior of a madman;
but those of the Tathāgata pacify all defects without exception.
Who here does not deserve to be honored? Consider this! || 5 ||
He who exerts himself for the slaughter of others, casting aside compassion; and he who, out of pity, engages in ritual acts for the sake of protection;
he who is possessed by passion, and he who is liberated from passion—[all these are alike].
Of these two, who here is to be honored? Reflecting upon this, speak.
Śakra, the wielder of the thunderbolt; Bala, the wielder of the plow; Kṛṣṇa, whose weapon is the discus;

Skanda, the wielder of the spear; Rudra, who dwells in the cremation ground and whose weapon is the trident—these childish ones, devoid of compassion, afflicted by the fear of suffering, and bearing various weapons.
What wise person would pay homage to those who are constantly raising their weapons, intent on the slaughter of living beings? (7)
He who bears neither a trident nor a fair-faced young woman upon his lap;
who holds neither a discus, nor a spear, nor a fierce thunderbolt, nor a plow;
and who, liberated from all afflictions, has a mind intent on accomplishing the welfare of others— [to him I bow].
I have come for refuge to that sage, the protector of the worlds.
Rudra carries a woman out of passion; Viṣṇu is devoid of shame; Skanda is exceedingly cruel and of ungrateful conduct; he himself is a slayer of his own kinsmen; Umā is cruel;
the Mothers are eaters of human fat, marrow, and flesh; and they are the destroyers of Mahiṣa.
And since the Guide desires to drink, what fault could there be, however slight, in the One Possessing Ten Powers? (9)
That Blessed One is not my kinsman, nor are the others my enemies; indeed, not even one among them has been seen by me in person.
Yet, having heard the power of their excellent conduct and sublime speech—
We have taken refuge in the Buddha out of a longing for his preeminent qualities. || 10 ||
Also in the *Saddharmaparikathā*:
"The Sugata is not our father, nor are the heretics our enemies; no wealth was given to us by that Tathāgata, nor has anything been taken away by Kaṇāda and the others."
But rather, because that Blessed One, the Buddha, is solely intent on the welfare of the world, and because his speech is stainless and removes all stains, we are devoted to him. (11)
He who is always and constantly a well-wisher and a benefactor of the world, by whom the health of the world afflicted by manifold diseases has been restored,
and whose entire object of knowledge he clearly perceives as if it were in the palm of his hand.
With devoted minds, take refuge in that virtuous and peerless sage.
Those who pay homage to that moon among the lords of sages, whether with incomplete devotion, by chance, through conformity to others, or out of doubt—
They too attain the prosperity of the immortals. || 13 ||
This is an ancient scriptural tradition: it is said that this Buddha, honored by the world, was formerly Hari;
seeing the world subject to birth, old age, and destruction, he exerted himself out of compassion.
Born into the excellent Śākya clan, Gautama, the Protector of men and possessor of wondrous intellect, is indeed the Teacher of benefit; what deluded person does not know him now? (14)
When,
devoid of *māyā*, his mind was intent on seizing the earth, he carried off the jewels of the *asuras* and *suras* out of passion and hatred.
At that time, even Hari is worthy of worship and salutation, for he is not liberated due to his lack of awakening;
a person abounding in delusion does not bow to the Buddha who is free from ignorance. || 15 ||
Having surrendered to Hari the earth, languid from the burden of her girdle-like four oceans and her rugged slopes, Bali fell into a wretched state;
yet King Aśoka, by giving even a mere handful of dust to a sage, attained freedom from sorrow.
He reached the earth, whose garment was the orb of the full moon and the sky. || 16 ||
I have no partiality for the Buddha, nor do I harbor hatred toward Kapila and others; rather, I accept the teaching of whichever teacher’s words are endowed with reason. (17)
Necessarily, whoever among all the Victors possesses a teaching that is vast and solely intent on the welfare of the world— he alone is to be sought by those with the subtle eye of intelligence.
And he is to be served; what [use] with those who are "wise" in what is meaningless? || 18 ||
He in whom no faults whatsoever exist and in whom all virtues are found—
whether he be Brahmā, Viṣṇu, or Maheśvara— he is my teacher.
I have gone for refuge to him in whom no faults are found and who possesses immeasurable virtues; he is omniscient and compassionate. (20)
Thus praised, O Buddha, whose wide lotus-petal eyes are like an ocean to the rivers of a thousand hymns—
whatever merit there may be in me arising from these words, [may it be for the benefit of all beings].
May all sentient beings be happy through that. || 21 ||
The *Devatāvimarśastuti* composed by the venerable teacher Śaṅkarasvāmin is completed.
